sentence:
We wish to count the numbers n in {1, 2, …, 300} that have both of these properties:
 
(1) n is the product of two distinct primes (i.e. n is square‐free with exactly two prime factors),
(2) n occurs as the “longer leg” (that is, the leg whose length is greater than that of the other non‐hypotenuse side) in a nondegenerate right triangle with all three side lengths integral (i.e. n is one of the legs in some Pythagorean triple and in that triple it is the larger leg).
sentence-category-reason: Restates the problem and specifies the two required properties to be counted.

sentence: A little thought shows that in any right–triangle with integer sides the hypotenuse is the longest side.
sentence-category-reason: States a general property about right triangles used for reasoning.

sentence: Moreover, one of the legs in a primitive triple is even and the other is odd, and when one “scales” a primitive triple the order (which leg is larger) does not change.
sentence-category-reason: Recalls structural facts about primitive triples and scaling, informing the reasoning.

sentence: In fact one may show that in every primitive triple the longer leg is an odd number.
sentence-category-reason: Asserts a deduced property that the longer leg in a primitive triple is odd.

sentence: (For example, in the well–known triple 6–8–10 the legs are 6 (even) and 8 (even) but this is not primitive; in the primitive 3–4–5 the odd leg is 3 but it turns out that when one “arranges” the standard parametrization the odd number appears as the larger leg if and only if a certain inequality is satisfied.
sentence-category-reason: Provides examples and explanatory remarks about parametrization and leg parity/order.

sentence: ) One may prove (by a short “factoring‐argument”) that if an integer occurs as a leg in some triple then it occurs as the larger leg in one and only one way.
sentence-category-reason: States a uniqueness property about an integer occurring as the larger leg.

sentence: In our situation this extra uniqueness and “ordering” implies that only odd numbers can appear as the longest leg of a right triangle with integer sides.
sentence-category-reason: Draws a logical consequence that only odd numbers can be longest legs.

sentence: Thus, among numbers n that are the product of two distinct primes, we must restrict to those that are odd.
sentence-category-reason: Narrows the set to odd semiprimes based on prior deductions.

sentence: (Notice that if one of the two primes were 2 then n would be even; a short investigation shows that numbers of the form 2 · q do occur in Pythagorean triples as a leg but it is always the shorter leg.
sentence-category-reason: Explains why even semiprimes (including factor 2) correspond to the shorter leg.
Sets notation and constraints by denoting n = pq with odd primes and p < q.

sentence: A useful (though not completely “obvious‐at‐first‐sight”) fact is that an odd number L occurs as the longer leg of a primitive triple if and only if the “smaller” of the two factors p and q (when L is square–free) is “not too small” relative to the other.
sentence-category-reason: States a criterion relating L as longer leg to a relative size condition of its prime factors.

sentence: (There is a fun “divisor–pair” argument that goes roughly as follows.
sentence-category-reason: Announces the plan to present a divisor-pair argument.

sentence: Suppose a right triangle has legs L and x (with L > x) and hypotenuse y.
sentence-category-reason: Introduces variables and assumptions for the triangle to carry out the argument.

sentence:
Then
  L² + x² = y²  ⟹  y² – x² = L²  ⟹  (y – x)(y + x) = L².
sentence-category-reason: Performs algebraic transformations leading to a factorization.

sentence: Now write d = y – x and e = y + x.
sentence-category-reason: Introduces substitutions for the factors to proceed with the argument.

sentence: Since y and x are integers the two factors d and e must have the same parity.
sentence-category-reason: Infers parity of the factors based on integer conditions.

sentence:
Moreover, one obtains
  x = (e – d)/2  and  y = (d + e)/2.
sentence-category-reason: Derives expressions for x and y in terms of d and e.

sentence:
For the triangle to be nondegenerate we need x > 0 (so e > d) and also x < L (since L is the longer leg) which leads to
  e – d < 2L.
sentence-category-reason: Derives inequality constraints from nondegeneracy and ordering.

sentence:
For a square–free L the nine divisors of L² are “spread out” and it turns out that one may find a solution with e – d < 2L if (and for our numbers, essentially only if) the two primes obey a condition equivalent to q < (√2 + 1) p; since √2 + 1 ≈ 2.414 the up‐shot is that for L = p · q we must have 
  q/p < 2.414.
sentence-category-reason: Concludes a necessary (essentially sufficient) inequality on q/p from divisor spacing.

sentence: A little algebra shows that with L = p q this necessary (and in fact sufficient) condition is equivalent to requiring that one of the non–trivial divisors of L² (namely, p²) lies in the interval (L(√2 – 1), L).
sentence-category-reason: States an equivalent condition framed via location of p^2 among divisors, as an algebraic observation.

sentence:
Thus, one may prove that if L = p · q (with 3 ≤ p < q) is to appear as the longest leg in some triple then we must have
 
  p² > (√2 – 1) (p q)   ⟹  p > (√2 – 1) q  ⟹  q < (1/(√2 – 1)) p.
sentence-category-reason: Derives and presents inequality conditions for L = pq to be the longest leg with logical implications.
Performs a concrete simplification and numerical approximation of 1/(√2−1).

sentence: Therefore, there are 13 integers n between 1 and 300 that are the product of two distinct primes and occur as the longer leg of some right triangle with integer side lengths.
